\subsection{The model system: a PbTiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ ferroelectric superlattice}
\label{sec:sample}

The test object is a relaxed atomistic supercell of a PbTiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ (PTO/STO)
ferroelectric superlattice --- $70.0\times70.0\times47.9$\,\AA, $19{,}440$ atoms ($1944$
PbTiO$_3$ and $1944$ SrTiO$_3$ formula units). Both materials are perovskites (ABO$_3$):
heavy Pb or Sr on the A-site, Ti on the B-site, oxygen on an octahedral cage. In the PTO
layers the B-site titanium and the A-site lead displace from their centrosymmetric
positions, giving each cell an electric dipole; the dipoles order into the swirling polar
domains --- vortices and labyrinth patterns --- characteristic of these superlattices
\citep{Yadav2016,Tang2015}. Figure~\ref{fig:sample}(a) shows this polarisation field,
computed here as the B-site off-centring relative to the A-site cage; (b) shows the atomic
columns in projection, where the polar displacement is directly visible as a splitting of
the lead columns into dumbbells.

This makes an exacting test for the localisation problem of Sec.~\ref{sec:atomfind} for
three reasons: (i) the scattering contrast spans two orders of magnitude, from lead
($Z=82$) to oxygen ($Z=8$), so the light sublattice sits near the noise floor; (ii) the
signal of interest is a \emph{sub-\aa{}ngstr\"om} displacement of atoms $1.9$--$3.9$\,\AA{}
apart; and (iii) the polarisation varies along the beam as well as across it, so the
structure is only fully recovered by a \emph{depth-resolved} method --- a projection image
integrates the very variation to be measured. The known input coordinates are the ground
truth against which every reconstructed and localised position is scored.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/sample}
  \caption{The PbTiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ model. (a) Ferroelectric polarisation (B-site
    off-centring relative to the A-site cage, mid-depth slab; arrow colour = in-plane
    direction), showing the polar domains; the dashed box is the $20$\,\AA{} scan window.
    (b) Atomic columns in beam projection within the scan region --- Pb, Sr, Ti and O ---
    with the overfocused probe ($\approx4$\,\AA) overlaid; the lead columns split into
    polar dumbbells.}
  \label{fig:sample}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Scanning transmission electron microscopy and 4D-STEM ptychography}
\label{sec:stem}

In scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) a convergent electron probe is focused
to a sub-\aa{}ngstr\"om spot and rastered across the specimen; at each position the
transmitted electrons are recorded \citep{PennycookNellist2011}. In \emph{four-dimensional}
STEM (4D-STEM) the point detector is replaced by a pixelated one that captures the entire
convergent-beam diffraction pattern at every probe position, yielding a four-dimensional
dataset $I(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k})$ --- two real-space scan axes $\mathbf{r}_p$ and two
reciprocal-space detector axes $\mathbf{k}$ \citep{Ophus2019,Tate2016}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:technique}a).

The reconstruction is \emph{ptychography}: recovery of the complex specimen transmission
from the diffraction patterns of a set of mutually overlapping illuminations
\citep{Hoppe1969,Nellist1995}. A single diffraction pattern discards the phase; the
information that restores it is the \emph{redundancy} between neighbouring probe positions.
Where two illuminations overlap in real space, their diffracted cones overlap in reciprocal
space, and the intensity in that overlap is an interference between the two --- its fringes
encode the phase gradient of the object (Fig.~\ref{fig:technique}b). Equivalently, as the
probe steps by an amount far smaller than its own width, features in the diffraction pattern
shift in a parallax that fixes their depth and phase. Solving the ensemble of overlapping
patterns jointly retrieves an object phase consistent with all of them
\citep{Rodenburg2008}, at a resolution set by the illumination angle rather than the lens
\citep{Nellist1995,Jiang2018}. Our step of $0.1$--$0.15$\,\AA{} against a $\approx4$\,\AA{}
probe gives ${>}90\%$ overlap --- heavy oversampling, which is what makes the phase problem
well-conditioned. The remainder of the Methods simulates this acquisition
(Sec.~\ref{sec:sim}) and inverts it (Sec.~\ref{sec:recon}).

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/technique}
  \caption{4D-STEM ptychography. (a) A convergent probe, here focused $20$\,\AA{} above the
    entrance surface (overfocus), diverges through the $\approx70$\,\AA{} specimen; a
    pixelated detector records the full diffraction pattern at each scan position.
    (b) Ptychographic redundancy: probe positions overlap strongly in real space (top), so
    their diffracted discs overlap in the detector plane (bottom) and interfere --- the
    fringes in the overlap encode the object phase.}
  \label{fig:technique}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Multislice 4D-STEM simulation}
\label{sec:sim}

\paragraph{The forward operator.}
The simulation is the forward model $\mathcal{S}$ mapping the known structure to the data a
microscope would record, $\mathbf{I}=\mathcal{S}(\{\mathbf{r}_a,Z_a\})+\text{noise}$. It
composes coherent multislice propagation, an incoherent average over thermal displacements,
and a photon-counting model. We state it explicitly because the reconstruction
(Sec.~\ref{sec:recon}) inverts the same operator, and the point-spread function used for
localisation (Sec.~\ref{sec:atomfind}) is the response of the composed forward--inverse pair
to a single atom.

\paragraph{Coherent multislice.}
At $300$\,keV the relativistic electron wavelength is
$\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_0 eU(1+eU/2m_0c^2)} = 1.969\times10^{-2}\,$\AA. The convergent probe is
the aperture-limited, aberrated source
\begin{equation}
  \psi_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{r};\mathbf{r}_p)
  = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\big\{A(\mathbf{k})\,e^{-i\chi(\mathbf{k})}\big\}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_p),
  \qquad \chi(\mathbf{k}) = \pi\lambda\,\Delta f\,\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert^2,
  \label{eq:probe}
\end{equation}
with $A$ the objective aperture ($A=1$ for $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert<\alpha/\lambda$), $\alpha=100$\,mrad
the convergence semi-angle, and $\chi$ kept to the defocus term (aberration-corrected
instrument), $\Delta f=-20$\,\AA{} a $20$\,\AA{} overfocus. The wave propagates through the
specimen by the multislice recursion \citep{CowleyMoodie1957,Kirkland2010},
\begin{equation}
  \psi_{n+1} = \mathcal{P}_{\Delta z}\!\otimes\!\big[\,t_n(\mathbf{r})\,\psi_n(\mathbf{r})\,\big],
  \qquad t_n(\mathbf{r}) = \exp\!\big[\,i\,\sigma\, v_n(\mathbf{r})\,\big],
  \label{eq:multislice}
\end{equation}
where each slice imprints a phase through its projected potential
$v_n(\mathbf{r})=\int_{z_n}^{z_n+\Delta z}V(\mathbf{r},z)\,\mathrm{d}z$, $\sigma=2\pi m e\lambda/h^2$
is the interaction constant, and $\mathcal{P}_{\Delta z}$ is the Fresnel propagator, i.e.\
multiplication by $\exp(-i\pi\lambda\Delta z\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert^2)$ in Fourier space. The
recorded quantity is the far-field exit-wave intensity
$I(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k})=\lvert\mathcal{F}\psi_N(\mathbf{k})\rvert^2$. We use abTEM
\citep{MadsenSusi2021} on GPU; projected potentials follow the constrained parameterisation
of \citet{LobatoVanDyck2014} at $\Delta z=2$\,\AA{} ($0.5$\,\AA{} for the finely sampled
runs). The full box is kept uncropped so the broadening exit wave does not alias at the
periodic boundaries.

\paragraph{Thermal diffuse scattering.}
Thermal motion is included in the frozen-phonon approximation \citep{LoaneXuSilcox1991},
valid because the electron transit time ($\sim\!10^{-16}$\,s) is far shorter than a phonon
period ($\sim\!10^{-12}$\,s): the measurement is the incoherent average of the intensity over
$N_\mathrm{ph}=16$ independently displaced configurations,
$I(\mathbf{k})=\langle\lvert\Psi(\mathbf{k})\rvert^2\rangle_{\mathbf{u}}\approx
N_\mathrm{ph}^{-1}\sum_j\lvert\Psi_j(\mathbf{k})\rvert^2$. The effect is quantified by the
Debye--Waller factor: for isotropic Gaussian displacements of one-dimensional variance
$\langle u^2\rangle$ and momentum transfer $\mathbf{q}$, the single-atom amplitude carries
\begin{equation}
  \big\langle e^{\,i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\big\rangle = e^{-M},\qquad
  M = \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert\mathbf{q}\rvert^2\langle u^2\rangle = B\,s^2,\quad
  s=\tfrac{\sin\theta}{\lambda},\; B=8\pi^2\langle u^2\rangle,
  \label{eq:dw}
\end{equation}
so the coherent intensity is attenuated by $e^{-2M}$, most strongly at high angle, and the
removed intensity re-emerges as a diffuse background (Fig.~\ref{fig:dw}). Because $M\propto B$
this is species-dependent, so displacement amplitudes are set \emph{per species} from
tabulated room-temperature isotropic $B$ \citep{Peng1996} --- passing the three-dimensional
magnitude $\sigma=\sqrt{3B/8\pi^2}$. Lead and oxygen vibrate roughly twice as far as titanium
($B_\mathrm{Pb}=0.90$, $B_\mathrm{O}=0.80$, $B_\mathrm{Sr}=0.55$, $B_\mathrm{Ti}=0.45$\,\AA$^2$);
a single averaged displacement would misweight the diffuse background of exactly the light
species hardest to detect.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.62\linewidth]{figs/debye_waller}
  \caption{Coherent surviving fraction $e^{-2M}$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:dw}) versus scattering angle for
    the four species at their room-temperature $B$; the complement (grey) is the thermal
    diffuse background. Heavier-vibrating Pb/O lose their coherent signal at lower angle than
    Ti, and oxygen's is additionally weak because $Z$ is small.}
  \label{fig:dw}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Detection and dose.}
The full $\approx200$\,mrad diffraction plane is recorded and binned $4\times4$ to
$356\times356$ pixels, keeping the zero-order disc centred so the reciprocal-space calibration
is exact. abTEM flux-normalises each pattern to $\tilde I$ ($\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\tilde I=1$); a
finite electron budget is imposed as a shot-noise model,
\begin{equation}
  n(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k}) \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\big(N_e\,\tilde I(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k})\big),
  \qquad N_e = D\,s_{\mathrm{scan}}^2,
  \label{eq:poisson}
\end{equation}
with $D$ the dose (e\,\AA$^{-2}$) and $s_{\mathrm{scan}}$ the scan step, so $N_e$ is the
electrons per pattern. Equation~\eqref{eq:poisson} is the likelihood the reconstruction is
matched to and that sets the statistical part of the localisation uncertainty; doses of
$10^{4}$--$10^{10}$\,e\,\AA$^{-2}$ span the coherent, near-noiseless reference to the
counting-limited regime.

\subsection{Multislice electron ptychographic reconstruction}
\label{sec:recon}

\paragraph{The inverse problem.}
Reconstruction inverts $\mathcal{S}$: from the recorded patterns it estimates the object by
iterative ptychography \citep{RodenburgFaulkner2004,Wakonig2020}. To resolve structure along
the beam the single multiplicative projection is replaced by a multislice object
\citep{MaidenHumphryRodenburg2012}: the specimen is a stack of $N_L$ transmission slices
$q_l(\mathbf{r})=\exp[i\sigma v_l(\mathbf{r})]$, and for a probe at $\mathbf{r}_j$ the model
exit wave is the same multislice operator $\mathcal{M}$ as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:multislice},
\begin{equation}
  \psi_j = \mathcal{M}\big[\{q_l\},\,P(\cdot-\mathbf{r}_j)\big],
  \qquad I_j^{\mathrm{model}}(\mathbf{k}) = \big\lvert\mathcal{F}\psi_j(\mathbf{k})\big\rvert^2 .
  \label{eq:ptycho_fwd}
\end{equation}
The unknowns are the slices $\{q_l\}$ and the probe, recovered jointly (Fig.~\ref{fig:ptycho}).
We reconstruct $N_L=70$ (coherent) or $105$ (thermally-averaged) slices across the
$\approx70$\,\AA{} thickness --- depth sampling $\Delta z_\mathrm{rec}\approx1.0$ and
$0.67$\,\AA{} --- with the hollow-detector inner angle set to zero so the full recorded cone
constrains the object.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/ptycho_inverse}
  \caption{Multislice ptychography as inversion of $\mathcal{S}$: the estimated probe and
    object slices generate a model pattern through the multislice operator $\mathcal{M}$; its
    amplitude is compared with the measurement and the residual drives a least-squares update
    of every slice and the probe.}
  \label{fig:ptycho}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Maximum-likelihood estimation.}
The estimate minimises a data-fidelity term equal to the negative log-likelihood of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:poisson}. PtychoShelves \citep{Wakonig2020} uses the least-squares
maximum-likelihood (LSQ-ML) engine of \citet{Odstrcil2018}, which in the shot-noise regime
reduces to the variance-stabilised amplitude metric
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{D}(\Theta) = \sum_{j}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}
  \Big(\sqrt{I_j^{\mathrm{model}}(\mathbf{k};\Theta)} - \sqrt{I_j^{\mathrm{meas}}(\mathbf{k})}\Big)^{2},
  \qquad \Theta=\big(\{q_l\},\{P_m\}\big),
  \label{eq:datafidelity}
\end{equation}
the Anscombe surrogate for the exact Poisson log-likelihood \citep{ThibaultGuizar2012}. The
reconstruction is therefore a maximum-a-posteriori estimate
$\hat\Theta=\arg\min_\Theta\mathcal{D}(\Theta)+\mathcal{R}(\Theta)$; \emph{we set $\mathcal{R}=0$
on the inter-layer coupling}, so the axial structure is set by the data rather than a
smoothness prior --- deliberately, since such a prior would bias the very axial coordinate we
later quantify. A two-stage schedule (a down-sampled $178$-pixel pre-solve, then a
full-resolution $356$-pixel refinement) accelerates convergence of the non-convex
$\mathcal{D}$.

\paragraph{Partial coherence and the probe.}
For the coherent reference a single fixed probe is used. For the thermally-averaged,
counting-limited data the illumination is a mixed state --- an incoherent sum of orthogonal
probe modes $\{P_m\}$ \citep{ThibaultMenzel2013} ---
$I_j(\mathbf{k})=\sum_m\lvert\mathcal{F}\,\mathcal{M}[\{q_l\},P_m(\cdot-\mathbf{r}_j)](\mathbf{k})\rvert^2$,
released after a single-mode burn-in. The extra incoherent degrees of freedom absorb the
thermal diffuse background and residual partial coherence that a single mode would otherwise
force into the coherent object, corrupting it; slow probe variation across the scan is further
accommodated by orthogonal probe relaxation \citep{Odstrcil2016}.

\paragraph{Depth resolution.}
Depth information is available because the overfocused probe propagates dynamically through a
specimen many times thicker than its depth of focus, and the multislice reconstruction
recovers that propagation slice by slice --- optical sectioning, not tomography. The axial
resolution is nonetheless bounded by the numerical aperture: in the limited-aperture
(single-orientation) regime the recoverable axial band scales as $\alpha^2/\lambda$, so
\begin{equation}
  \delta x \approx \frac{\lambda}{2\alpha}\approx 0.10\,\text{\AA},
  \qquad
  \delta z \approx \frac{\lambda}{\alpha^2}\approx 2.0\,\text{\AA}.
  \label{eq:resolution}
\end{equation}
The reconstructed response of a single atom is correspondingly anisotropic --- tight in-plane,
elongated $\approx20\times$ along the beam. This elongation is a deterministic, correlated
uncertainty in the axial coordinate, not statistical scatter, so it neither averages away with
dose nor is captured by a residual-based error estimate; the response is measured directly and
used as the three-dimensional point-spread function of the localisation model
(Sec.~\ref{sec:atomfind}), which propagates the correlation explicitly.

\subsection{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}

All parameters are collected in Table~\ref{tab:params}. The simulation
(\texttt{simulate\_4dstem.py}, abTEM~1.0.x) and the reconstruction driver (PtychoShelves, the
\texttt{GPU\_MS} multislice engine) are scripted end to end; the data contract between them
is the PtychoShelves worked-example format (diffraction stack, scan positions, and initial
probe), with a fixed transpose ($\texttt{custom\_data\_flip}=[0,0,1]$) relating the
reconstructed and model frames. Code, the input structure, and the exact per-run parameters
are in the project repository, so a run is reproduced by regenerating the data from the
structure and re-running the driver with the tabulated values.
